title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
authors: Daniel Lovsted, Filipa C. R. Peres, Joshua Nevin, Selman Ipek, Anne Broadbent
abstract: Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.
summary: This paper presents significant advancements in Blind Quantum Computation (BQC), addressing the major bottleneck of server resource scaling. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC) and introducing an entanglement-based dual protocol, the authors drastically reduce the required quantum server size. The work also provides rigorous security proofs, confirming the perfect security of the delegated computation scheme.
main_problem: The primary challenge in Blind Quantum Computation (BQC) is the server resource cost, which historically scales poorly with the computation size.
main_result: The authors propose a protocol using Pauli-based computation (PBC) that reduces the required server size to depend only on the non-Clifford T gate count, and they introduce an entanglement-based dual protocol for further resource reduction.
method: The work develops and analyzes three-stage protocols (Preparation, Measurement, Output) involving random Pauli rotations and classical post-processing to simulate quantum computation securely.
model_or_system: The model is the secure delegation of quantum computation (BQC) from a low-resource client to a quantum server, utilizing Pauli operators and resource state preparation.
key_observables: The server resource size (qubit count), the required measurement bases (Pauli-X and Y for the dual protocol), and the resulting density matrices ($ho_k$).
important_parameters: The non-Clifford T gate count ($t$), the number of qubits ($n$), and the security condition requiring indistinguishable quantum channels.
main_assumptions: The security proof relies on establishing the perfect indistinguishability of quantum channels using an auxiliary protocol (Auxiliary BPBC) and assuming the ability to perform specific single-qubit Pauli measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the three stages of PBC and Blind PBC, and a separate figure details the entanglement-based dual protocol (TRC) involving preparation and adaptive measurement.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the core PBC protocol, then introducing the resource-optimized dual protocol (TRC), and finally dedicating significant sections to proving the perfect security of the underlying protocols using density matrix analysis and inductive proofs.
why_interesting: The focus on resource scaling and the development of provably secure, resource-efficient protocols for delegated quantum computation are central theoretical topics in quantum information theory.
